title: PARRY modelled beliefs, judged new statements as fitting or threatening them, then chose how to resp
description:
Stanford psychiatrist who built PARRY to simulate paranoid schizophrenia

PARRY modelled beliefs, judged new statements as fitting or threatening them, then chose how to respond. Contemporaries called it "ELIZA with attitude": a real conversational strategy, not just pattern-matched replies.

In an early-1970s trial, experienced psychiatrists questioned real patients and PARRY over teleprinters; a separate panel of 33 psychiatrists then read the transcripts blind. Teleprinters, not chat windows: this predates the personal computer by nearly a decade.

correct guesses at telling PARRY from a real patient, statistically no better than chance.

PARRY and ELIZA even talked to each other over ARPANET at a 1972 computer conference. Two scripted programs, simulating a therapist and a patient, having a conversation neither could actually understand.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PARRY: confirms Kenneth Colby, a Stanford psychiatrist, wrote PARRY in 1972 to simulate paranoid schizophrenia; that it modelled beliefs and a conversational strategy, described as "ELIZA with attitude"; the early-1970s trial in which psychiatrists questioned real patients and PARRY over teleprinters while a separate panel of 33 psychiatrists read transcripts blind, correctly identifying human versus machine only 48% of the time (consistent with chance); and that PARRY and ELIZA were connected over ARPANET at the 1972 ICCC conference.
